195.text: Cast INT8 to float, multiply by scale, then do the matrix multiply. Mathematically: x @ (W_int8 * scale)^T. The approximation error is small because neural network weights are typically well-distributed.

276.text: Size reduction is the one claim in this lab that does not depend on the machine, so it is the one worth asserting. The speed figure is deliberately left unguarded, because it is a property of the host rather than of quantization.

287.text: Size and speed are the easy numbers. The one that decides whether you can ship a quantized model is how far the weights moved, so measure it per layer instead of asserting that INT8 is 'close enough'.

288.text: Report max|W|, the scale, the worst absolute error, and that error as a percentage of the layer's largest weight. The percentage is the portable column: it should come out the same for every layer, and if it does not, something is wrong with the scale.

290.text: Grab the FP32 weights by module name before quantizing, so each quantized layer can be compared against the exact tensor it came from. Names line up because quantize_model replaces children in place.

296.text: Round-trip the INT8 weights back through the scale and compare with the original. This is the error the model actually sees at inference rather than a theoretical bound, since the forward pass performs this same dequantization on every call.

297.text: Take the worst element, not the mean. An average error would be reassuring and useless: what breaks a quantized model is the outlier weight, which is exactly why production schemes go per-channel.

300.text: Every layer prints at about 0.394% of its own max|W|. The constancy is the point: symmetric per-tensor quantization has a fixed relative cost, and the differences between layers are entirely differences in weight range.

302.text: The measured numbers match the closed form: rounding to a grid of step scale bounds the error at scale/2 = max|W|/254, which is where the 0.4% comes from. Theory and measurement agreeing is the cheapest sanity check available.

309.text: Weight error is only interesting if it reaches the predictions. Per-token cross-entropy on names the model never trained on is the standard way to ask that, and it is the comparison this lab previously promised without making.

317.text: reduction="sum" with an explicit token count, rather than averaging per name. Otherwise short names would count as much as long ones and the figure would drift with the length distribution instead of the weights.

323.text: Training walked docs[0:num_steps], so everything past that index is genuinely unseen. A held-out set carved out of the same shuffle costs nothing and is the difference between a loss number and a memorization check.

325.text: The same names scored under the INT8 model. Both models see identical inputs in identical order, so the delta is attributable to the rounded weights and nothing else.

328.text: The delta comes out around +0.0001 nats, roughly six thousandths of a percent. That answers 'does INT8 hurt this model' with a number and a sign rather than a shrug.

343.text: Generates n names from each model off one seed and pairs them up. Sampling both models under the same seed is what makes this a comparison at all: any difference in the output then has to come from the weights.

352.text: Reset the RNG before each model so FP32 and INT8 draw the identical stream of uniforms out of torch.multinomial. Without this the two lists would differ for reasons that have nothing to do with quantization.

357.text: Two seeds, and the second one is the whole point. Seed 42 produces identical lists and seed 1 does not. Printing only the first would invite the reader to conclude that INT8 reproduces FP32 exactly, which is false.

368.text: Ten names off one seed cannot support a claim either way, so sweep 40 seeds. Roughly one name in six differs. That rate, not either listing above, is the honest summary of what INT8 costs the output.
